About this citation

The text of a public lecture, published at the request of the audience, and Sartre later said he regretted its formulation — particularly the phrase about existence preceding essence, and the reading of 'we are free' that the lecture invites. It is nonetheless the source of most of his most-quoted lines.

#### About Jean-Paul Sartre

Jean-Paul Sartre (1905–1980) was the public face of French existentialism, author of Being and Nothingness, plays, novels, and political essays. Captured in World War II, he later co-founded Les Temps modernes and refused the 1964 Nobel Prize.

### Interpretation

Sartre's claim is that freedom is not a property people have but the condition they are in. "Condemned" means there is no opting out: even refusing to choose is a choice one is answerable for. In his framework existence precedes essence — there is no human nature to serve as excuse or as script — so what a person is comes entirely from what they do. The sentence is meant to be unsettling rather than liberating, since the responsibility it describes cannot be transferred.

#### Why it matters

It removes a familiar refuge. "I had no choice" is rarely literally true, and treating it as true is itself the thing Sartre is describing.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Man is condemned to be free.”?

“Man is condemned to be free.” comes from Existentialism Is a Humanism (1946), attributed to Jean-Paul Sartre.

#### What does Jean-Paul Sartre mean by freedom?

Philosophers distinguish several ideas under the single word freedom. Negative freedom emphasizes non-interference; positive freedom emphasizes the capacity to act according to reasons, virtue, or authentic desire. This passage enters that discussion through freedom, responsibility, choice.
